item.title: 📈 Monday data: Damming the slop floods
item.description: AI makes content cheap. Who pays to make it trustworthy?
item.content:encoded:
There’s a flood of AI content coming down the pipeline across all forms of media. Music, images, LinkedIn posts, longform, and book summaries. As AI output grows, the question becomes: what does a future coexistence with AI-generated content look like?

The growth of websites made by AI has been noticeable since 2023. Now every third webpage created has some part attributable to AI.

Press releases, expected to be a trustworthy source of information, hit an all-time high of nearly a 50% chance of containing AI-generated text in June this year — doubling within a year. AI-generated content and assistance are becoming normalized.

Infinite AI content, finite demand?

AI-generated content is not limited to websites and articles, either. The cost of making a music track has dropped so much that, at its peak in June, over half of new music sent to Deezer, a streaming platform, was fully AI-generated.

Yet, no one seems to be listening. AI tracks account for just 1-3% of the streams.

It’s too early to tell whether this is due to taste or discovery – and we should not infer that humans are not interested in AI music.

Audiences seem willing to engage with AI-powered content in the fiction space, and choose to pay.

Pocket FM, an Indian audio-drama app, says that AI powers 93% of its content1. Its catalog has grown to 2.5 million hours produced a year – from 100,000 hours just two years ago.

Revenue had initially stalled in the first six months of overhauling production with AI. The upturn came from feeding listener data back into the process2. Ninety-six titles, out of 770,000+, have now made the company more than $1 million each and doubled revenue in a year3.

Clearly not every title is a hit, but Pocket FM will be a useful test over the next year of where AI input in the creative process creates and retains value. If it does well, it might tell us that, for listeners, it doesn’t matter how content is produced as long as it makes for a good story.

Subscribe now

Slop dams

UK adults spend some 72 minutes a day consuming news. Just 8 minutes of that are spent accessing publishers directly online. Search, aggregators, AI, social media and video-sharing platforms together account for 37%.

Direct exposure to publishers may decline even further.

Since Google’s AI Overviews launched in May 2024, small publishers have been the most affected by the piping in the internet’s infrastructure. Even the largest sites lost 22% of their Google referral traffic.

Distributors govern entry to platforms and audience discovery. DistroKid handles ~40% of all new music, focused on self-releasing artists, receiving new submissions and pushing them to your favorite music library. At the same time, it hasn’t signed the industry’s anti-fraud standards, while 27 other music and industry bodies have.

Universal Music Group (UMG), the largest record label, is now suing DistroKid for allegedly giving platforms and listeners the impression they are getting legitimate music while distributing mass-generated AI content4. UMG is not against clearly disclosed AI music. They seem to take issue with what listeners believe is authentic.

When Deezer found that in 2025, up to 85% of streams on AI-generated tracks were fraudulent plays, they turned that capability into a business by licensing the AI-detection technology.

The verification budget

Music is one of the first, but should not be the last to define what standard is acceptable. Who gets to define what counts as useful AI and whether it should reach audiences?

At least $240 million has gone into shaping AI rules and regulations across four disclosed funds in just over a year. AI auditing and certification is a fraction of the funding – and yet it’s the one area that could change how the AI content flood changes the human experience of the internet.

The open question is where the responsibility of verification lies. recently made the point when interviewed on Bloomberg5 that “the industry ought to be covering the costs of its own risks, liabilities and damage. That’s what we expect of every industry. And there’s enough money coming in.” Verification should make up part of the budget as a preventative measure.

We are entering a world where coexistence with AI-generated content is inevitable, whether in the form of functional content that we tolerate, or in the form of content that we enjoy or something we seek to filter out and avoid.

1

Pocket FM uses AI across writing assistance, adaptation, narration and production, while humans remain involved in originating ideas and stories.

2

See Feedback is the moat and Why AI isn’t showing up on your bottomline.

3

Annual revenue rate.

4

DistroKid denies the allegations.

5

Interview starts 26 minutes in.

item.title: 🔮 Quick weekend reads: the big AI questions
item.description: A short set of readings on some of the biggest questions.
item.content:encoded:
AI is really forcing some big questions into the open. Here are some weekend reads on them.

The biggest idea

The Economist address the effective altruism (EA) belief system, which it calls “this century’s biggest idea”:

[P]lenty of EAs in Silicon Valley think that only they can be trusted with the technology. That is an alarming idea. Effective altruists’ argument for worrying about really powerful AIs is that the machines could optimise for a single and fatally wrong objective. Everyone should worry, too, about what happens when a small group of people fall into the same trap

The full analysis is worth reading. Also read the brief response by Alexander Berger, the CEO of Coefficient Giving, an EA-aligned philanthropist.

The religious angle

The New York Times reports that Anthropic had been consulting with religious scholars and theologians on the question of machine consciousness. Anthropic has prioritised questions of whether its systems might imbue consciousness and personhood more than other AI companies. It goes so far as Anthropic’s team proposed to withdraw from a Vatican event before the Pope’s encyclical Magnifica Humanitas argued that AIs “do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain… nor do they have a moral conscience.”

EV reader, Anil Seth’s X thread and the pushback he received are worth scanning.

These are huge questions. We’ll touch on consciousness in tomorrow’s newsletter.
Meanwhile, happy to hear your reasoned thoughts below.

item.title: 🔮 The transition is hiding in plain sight #604
item.description: AI consciousness, electrification’s hidden progress, and the coming agentic bank run++
item.content:encoded:
Good morning!

It’s been a whirlwind week. We had our first look inside a major AI company’s leaked IPO prospectus. Our data appeared in the FT’s explainer on tokenomics. We are continuing to push hard on untangling this data and more over at our AI Investment Brief by Exponential View.

Subscribe now

Further along than it looks

The electrification of the world economy is further ahead than most people think. Data from the International Energy Agency show that electricity now powers 46% of global GDP. Yet it makes up only 23% of the final energy we use.

Which bar you watch determines how far along you think we are. Focus tends to be on final energy because the 77% of final energy that remains unelectrified is where most of the emissions sit. But that understates the progress we have made so far. If we measure electricity by the value it generates, rather than how much we use, the transition looks much further along.

The reason for the gap – and much of electricity’s value – is that it’s a more efficient technology. A gasoline car turns about 25% of its fuel into motion. An electric car can do it at 85-90% efficiency (and makes far less noise). It’s the same story across the economy, where a joule of electricity does about 2.5 times as much useful work as a joule of oil.

See also: Momentum is still building! In Norway, vans and heavy-duty vehicles are following the move to electric. Once one adjacent technology blazes the trail others can quickly follow.

A MESSAGE FROM OUR SPONSOR

AI ISN’T THE REAL ADVANTAGE

AI is everywhere in the enterprise. But Tempo’s latest research shows the advantage is not. To understand why, they spoke to senior leaders already using AI at scale to plan and run complex portfolios.

They found that legacy portfolio platforms built for a human workforce are struggling. Yet, only a fraction of teams use AI capabilities end‑to‑end – and they’re already outperforming their peers by a remarkable margin.

Tempo’s report shows how to turn AI into your advantage.

Download report

Could AI be conscious?

Yes, no, maybe. It’s a bit of an unanswerable question, but a new paper from Google DeepMind takes a good crack at mapping the landscape. (Props to EV readers Shamil Chandaria and Anil Seth for co-authoring the work.)

The first problem is one you may have hit at 3am on a college couch: no one agrees on what produces consciousness. Some researchers think the right kind of computer could be conscious. Others say it needs a body. Kookier still, some think experience is woven into all matter (rocks included). The second problem is that even people who share a theory can disagree about whether AI shows the right signs.

To bring some clarity, the authors fold this debate into a five-level framework that captures many theories about how to assess consciousness:

  1. observing a system’s behavior

  2. examining the algorithms it runs

  3. examining the wiring of its hardware

  4. asking whether it’s a living thing with something at stake (for example, its own life)

  5. examining how it’s connected to the world

Each level comes with markers you can test an AI against. Today’s AI does fairly well on the first level, patchily on the second, and abysmally on the last three. You can try it yourself with the paper’s interactive map. Our team’s scores ranged from 0.003 to 0.083 out of 1, so we lean firmly toward no. But those scores depend on the theories we picked. Until there’s better evidence for which theory is right, the honest answer to whether AI is conscious remains: maybe.

See also: a great cartoon explaining the paper.

Hey Siri, make me $1 million

As personal agents like Muse, Grok Bot and dots land in our pockets, they’ll start optimizing daily life in lots of small ways. My gym lets me pause my membership for three months a year, and I never do. An agent would pause it every time I went away.

Another area where it could help is managing my money. Most people don’t have the time or expertise to move money between bank accounts in search of better rates. But they can: neobanks offer higher yields on deposits than most banks do.

Torsten Sløk, chief economist at the asset manager Apollo, asks what happens when every household’s agent starts moving that money. Banks rely on a large pool of cheap, idle deposits to fund their lending. If agents routinely sweep that cash into higher-paying accounts, banks’ funding costs will rise. Sløk calls it an “agentic bank run.”

Subscribe now

Short morsels to appear smart at dinner parties

🎞️ The best copy of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly owes its existence to amateur pirates who spent years building illegal bootlegs of the movie.

🏙️ What’s the best shape for a city? Compact and dense. The interactive model is fun to play with.

💘 The Singapore government is running its own dating service using the Gale-Shapley algorithm, which, in theory, leaves no two people who would both rather be with each other than with their matches. Romance, optimized.

🤖 OpenAI has released dots, its competitor to Grok Bot. Meanwhile, SpaceXAI owns dot.com, which redirects to the Grok Bot download page.

🌀 Brain waves, long dismissed as background noise produced by neurons, may help coordinate thinking.

🖥️ A good read: a brief history of the Bloomberg Terminal, the nervous system of global finance.

📰 AI models bury bad news unless told not to.

🇪🇺 Google, Apple and Amazon each hold more meetings with EU officials than any single European company.

Thanks for reading!

item.title: 🔮 AI & Math 2.0, Pakistan’s solar hedge & who controls computing++
item.description: An essential weekly reading on AI.
item.content:encoded:
“I’ve worked in the tech industry for the last 10 years, and Exponential View has guided me and helped me think much larger than I otherwise would have.” — Nicky B., a paying member

Subscribe now

Hi all,

Welcome to the Sunday edition #605.

If you’re catching up this weekend, we covered a lot of ground on AI adoption, long-term knowledge impact, agent economics, and chip innovation during the week. If you missed anything, we’ve gathered this week’s Exponential View and AI Investment Brief readings at the end.

Enjoy!

A MESSAGE FROM OUR SPONSOR

Granola unlocked today’s post for you.

We use Granola to capture our meetings. See it in action in the notes from our latest AI Investment Brief members’ call. Join EV as an annual member and get four months of Granola Business for free, with 10 seats for your team.

Go annual, get Granola

Math 2.0

When OpenAI released its repo with hundreds of mathematical manuscripts and supporting proofs, I asked what it might mean for the future of human knowledge:

Problems that have stumped the best human minds for decades fell to one afternoon of compute. […] Back in 1794, Condorcet bet that knowledge and our capacity to spread it and share it would evolve together. He has been right for nearly three hundred years. Now they might be coming apart, but not because of the intrinsic nature of these discoveries. We could bring them together if we insist our AI systems provide explanations, not merely proofs.

If we don’t, we’ll have more answers and less understanding.

A new group calling itself the Association for Human Mathematics criticized the release and called on mathematicians to stop working with OpenAI. Here I tend to agree with that there isn’t a “way to unring the bell, nor do I think we would ever go back to the old ways of doing maths.”

Terence Tao is pragmatic in his vision for Math 2.0:

“Math 1.0” placed a premium on being the first to solve an open problem, even if the solution was not initially well understood. Now that this goal has been optimized to the point of unsustainability, “Math 2.0” will need to decenter the role of raw problem solving and value mathematical progress more holistically - for instance by elevating the role of exposition, but also that of community building and opening up new directions of study. I believe that AI can contribute positively in all of these directions as well; but it will require more imagination and ambition…

The transition is hitting the field hard; after all, an open problem can organize years of training and collaboration at institutions. In a seminar this week, Fields medallist Hugo Duminil-Copin says his PhD students and postdocs were “in a state of total panic”. Like Tao, he calls for community-building — working with colleagues and students to understand the results, organizing conferences, and writing explanations for a wider community.

See also:

  • In cryptocurrency circles, Justin Drake urges preparation for “bunker mode,” warning that AI could undermine the digital signatures that authorize transactions before quantum computers do; calls it a “sobering moment” for the industry.

  • An independent researcher used AI coding tools to investigate a possible new planet. Amateurs have contributed to astronomy before AI, but with new tools, they might take on more research, while experts focus on even bigger, currently dormant problems.

  • ’s State of AI Report 2026 is out – it’s an important reference, worth your time.

  • McKinsey has a useful systems view of the AI economy.

    Subscribe now

More than chips

I worked with the WEF1 to release The Next-Generation Computing Framework this week. Compute is a condition of economic participation and strategic infrastructure. For me, that puts some practical questions ahead of the excitement for governments and firms, including:

  1. Sovereignty needs a practical test. A country can own its data centers and still depend on a foreign supplier for anything from maintenance to licensing. We can no longer assume peacetime. We recommend testing agency in the supply chain, “stress-testing whether autonomy actually exists in moments of crisis, rather than relying on peacetime assumptions of access,” to understand what happens when those suppliers become unavailable.

  2. Next-generation computing needs an energy plan. Quantum computing still depends on conventional computers for control, error correction, and processing results. They will likely sit alongside existing infrastructure, potentially increasing total electricity demand.

  3. Find the constraint before spending more on compute. Our framework treats electricity, data, or skills constraints as potential limits on what other investments can achieve. More computing capacity may have limited value if people cannot put it to work — so we advise solving the constraints before spending more on compute.

Read the white paper here.

Pakistan, electrified

We’ve followed Pakistan’s rooftop solar revolution since 2024, and in March examined how it was cushioning the country against imported-fuel shocks with the Strait of Hormuz closing.

Now high fuel prices could accelerate another change for Pakistan. The government targeted 30% of all new vehicle sales to be electric by 2030. This week, government adviser Haroon Akhtar told Bloomberg that higher petrol prices could bring that target forward.

The transition in developing nations, however, remains “chaotic and unequal,” as points out. The grid’s costs don’t disappear when customers buy less electricity. If those fixed costs are recovered through higher electricity prices, households that can’t afford panels may get higher bills. A cheaper alternative for some can make the shared system more expensive for others.

See also:

  • Energy researcher Seaver Wang argues that a bipartisan permitting deal could substantially benefit clean energy even if it also helps fossil-fuel projects. About 85% of the generation and storage capacity awaiting US grid connections is solar, wind, or batteries.

Subscribe now

Short morsels to appear smart at dinner parties

Why are personal agents taking off in the US, but not in China? points at China’s mobile superapp ecosystem.

In a retrospective study of over 54,000 women, AI picked up a rising cancer risk signal years before diagnosis.

🔋😎 A review of 157 experimental studies finds that retired batteries can still have much to give. Of more than 10,000 retired cells, median remaining capacity was 84.5%.

has cataloged 160 new drug programs cleared to begin human trials in China this year.

🧱 Researchers created a semi-autonomous AI system that can build new materials atom by atom.

A Canadian startup is deploying permafrost blankets in the Arctic.

🎩 Victorian Britain’s ruling class was successful despite living what, to us, may look like a frivolous life. An amusing read.

A new typeface inspired by Michelangelo’s manuscripts is coming to Word.

AI can take binary files of two games and fuse them together – think Super Mario running around Dark Souls.

The latest from our team:

In Exponential View:

  • More AI, more justice? — Can AI help people navigate the legal system without a lawyer?

  • What is left to do — What happens when machines make discoveries faster than we can understand them?

  • The end of screen time — left his laptop behind and discovered how much work he can do by talking to AI.

In AI Investment Brief, we examined:

  • AI revenues at $276bn annualized — Our updated accounting of the money coming into AI.

  • Economic agents — What would it cost to run a persistent personal AI assistant?

  • High-bandwidth flash — A proposed memory design that could help AI chips do more work.

Subscribe now

Thanks for reading!

1

I am a co-chair of the Global Future Council on Next Generation Computing.

item.title: 📈 What is bigger than AI?
item.description: GLP-1s: the science, the savings and the societal stakes.
item.content:encoded:
In August 2024, we said GLP-1s “will be the most impactful technology in the US over the next two years, with more meaningful and measurable impacts than either artificial intelligence or renewable technologies.”

Later, in October that year, we estimated its impact in the medical field alone could affect 20% of US adults, with another 6-10% using them for lifestyle reasons; in the final scenario we laid out, up to 60-70% of US adults, targeting dopamine addictions and desire regulation.

That year, 3% of US adults took a GLP-1 for weight loss; that’s now up to 11%. More than twice as many Americans pay for GLP-1s as pay for AI (via ).

Subscribe now

Bigger than the bots

By the end of 2025, GLP-1 sales exceeded generative AI revenue, reaching $76 billion, versus our $63 billion for generative AI. Revenue growth suggests this may be the crossover year.

The cost collapse

Semaglutide – the second-best-selling drug in the US last year – had a listed cost of $1,349 per month’s supply in the US on first release in June 2021. That hasn’t budged since. The cash price outside of insurance has dropped; Novo’s self-pay price came in at $499/month, and fell to as low as $199/month from February this year1.

When the patent in India expired on March 20 this year, the cost dropped further. A month’s supply is about $13,2 99% below the original US list price and 93% below the cash price.

Pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly is trading prices for volume; in Q2 this year, a 13% realized price cut drove a 60% volume boom3. Sales growth in India did not sustain after the generic release, with only 2% growth in June after monthly sales grew 58% in April.

Price cuts are well and good, but it’s not yet clear people are staying on them long term, as they’re meant to be. For instance, the FDA approved Wegovy in 2021 “for chronic weight management”, with no specified duration. GLP-1s taken for diabetes are also expected to be taken indefinitely, like other diabetes drugs.

However, in a Danish study of people using GLP-1s for obesity, half quit within a year. A UK study found 32% stayed on the drug after one year, and that dropped more than half to 15% after two years.

Injections aren’t the most convenient or comfortable. Over the last year, oral GLP-1s have started to enter the picture. A daily pill might be more sustainable than a weekly injection for maintaining results.

Subscribe now

Efficacy expanding, in places

As new products have been released, the performance on mean weight loss continues to improve for the weekly injectables. Over five years, we’ve seen a 10-percentage-point improvement in weight loss from semaglutide in 2021 to retatrutide this May. The pills have been less effective than the injections despite greater comfort for the user and being easier to manufacture.

The results aren’t always consistent, and as we pointed out in SNL#569, scientists now know that genetics plays a part in the outcome.

Beyond weight loss, researchers are further investigating a series of potentially life-changing, unrelated side effects. One study found semaglutide and talking therapy together cut heavy drinking days by 41% among adults with alcohol use disorder and obesity compared with 26% with therapy alone.

Similarly, GLP-1 use has been linked with 50% fewer deaths from substance abuse. In 2024, we described this as a “temperance technology” that helps change behaviors overall.

More wide-ranging impacts are debated. Heart aging is reported to have slowed by 2-4 years in high-risk individuals on semaglutide4. The authors argue that this isn’t fully attributable to weight loss, so another effect must be at play, though it remains inconclusive for now.

This doesn’t mean the same benefits would occur in a healthy population, but it shows we understand better what might be possible.

A MESSAGE FROM OUR SPONSOR

Risk = capability × access × autonomy × scale

AI doesn’t need to go rogue to cause harm. It “only” needs an objective, access to your systems, and the ability to move faster than you can spot it.

Box’s CISO, Heather Ceylan, thinks of this risk as capability × access × autonomy × scale. She argues that model guardrails help but aren’t enough to keep risks at bay. Firms also need audit trails, human approval for consequential actions, and limited permissions.

For security leaders and anyone building with AI, Heather shared a first-hand view of how to build innovation that can be trusted at scale.

Explore AI risk formula

Want to sponsor Exponential View? Email us.

Waiting on worldly change

On weight loss, GLP-1s are a formidable drug. Obesity in US adults peaked at nearly 40% in 2022 and was down three percentage points as measured up to July 2026. Simultaneously, the number of new diabetes diagnoses has flatlined. Not all of this can be attributed to taking GLP-1 drugs, despite them making up 14% of US drug spend in 20255.

It’s still unclear whether this translates into real-world differences outside the weight-loss world, with contradicting papers making the rounds. A Danish study found that users took 17% less long-term sick leave over four years—equivalent to $722 per employed user per year. Yet another study found that there were no medical cost savings for insurers over five years. In fact, medical spending rose by $0.22 for every $1 spent on GLP-1s.

In the UK, the change in shopping habits is a cut and a shift in spending: users spend less and switch from chocolate (down 18 percentage points) to gum and mouthwash (up 24 and 20 percentage points, respectively). Hershey is promoting gum and mints specifically to combat “Ozempic breath” and has seen nutrition bar sales grow 12% in Q2 this year.

The weight-management effects are real, but access can still be uneven. Four Medicaid programs in the US dropped GLP-1s for obesity this year, amid budget pressures. With semaglutide and tirzepatide patents not due to expire until 2032 and 2036, large price drops in the US are not likely for several years. This is a blip, not a hard constraint, however.

More than a health aid, GLP-1s are a temperance technology with wide societal impact. In a national simulation, those without a high school diploma would gain the most – 14% more lifetime social value, 16-17% more quality-adjusted years, and a 20% larger life expectancy gain than the average person; college graduates gained 15-27% less.

We expect GLP-1s to keep marching on.

Thanks for reading!

In the AI Investment Brief today: An update on the AI cycle status and the AI economy in September.

1

The average price is set at $350/month; the $199/month price applies to the first two doses.

2

The dosage is not directly comparable, as it is a lower dosage than the Wegovy obesity drug.

3

Lilly attributes most of the price fall to Mounjaro joining China’s state reimbursement list and a cut in the US cash price for Zepbound.

4

5
